abstract: |
  Transboundary haze from Indonesian peatland fires poses severe public health and environmental risks to Singapore, creating an operational need for early air quality forecasting ahead of smoke arrival. In this study, we tested five statistical and machine learning, including Elastic Net, Random Forest, Support Vector Regression (SVM), Vector Autoregressive Exogenous (VARX) and Spatial Autoregressive (SAR). They are used to predict regional PM2.5 concentrations in West Singapore one hour ahead (t+1hr) and six hours ahead (t+6hr) during the August–October 2019 haze episode. Hourly regional air quality readings are integrated with Cartesian wind velocity vectors and NASA satellite fire metrics from Sumatra. Models are evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE) over a chronological holdout window (21–31 October 2019). Results show that spatial and regularised linear models outperform non-linear tree ensembles. SAR and VARX(3) models achieved the lowest errors at t+1hr by capturing cross-regional diffusion, while linear SVM and VARX(3) models led at t+6hr. Spatial and causal diagnostics further confirm strong inter-regional dependence, with smoke surges entering from southern and western zones propagating across Singapore within 2 to 4 hours.

# Introduction
Transboundary haze from forest and peatland fires in Sumatra is a problem for Singapore, especially when weather gets dry. In September 2019, winds from the south carried smoke from Sumatra to Singapore. This led to a decline in air quality (Meteorological Service Singapore, 2020). High levels of pollution can affect health and life. Outdoor work, school activities and public events can all be affected.

As the haze conditions can change rapidly, relying on pollution readings may not give enough time for early preparation. This study therefore looks at historical regional air-quality measurements, meteorological conditions and satellite-detected fire activity in Sumatra can be used to forecast short-term PM$_{2.5}$ concentrations in Singapore, potentially supporting earlier public-health preparedness.

## Literature Review 
Traditional air quality forecasting approaches such as Multiple Linear Regression mainly rely on linear assumptions and have long served as standard baseline for air quality (Abdullah et al., 2020). Conversely, Machine Learning techniques account for non-linear relationships and time-lagged variables. Machine Leaning modeling frameworks such as Random Forest (RF), Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have started to emerge as a way to effectively predict air quality (Palanichamy et al., 2022). Futhermore, Spatial Autoregressive model such as Vector Autoregressive Exogenous systems and Spatial Autoregressive models can be used to model how pollutants diffuse across interconnected geographic locations. Thus, this project investigates several machine learning algorithms for forecasting haze levels in Singapore, ultimately providing relevant information to responsible parties which allows them to mitigate and plan precautionary measures. 

## Problem Statement 
The problem statement centers on the operational challenge faced by public health authorities, which is mitigating the reporting latency between smoke generated by Indonesia and public health advisories in Singapore. Without predictive tools, authorities risk reacting only after the haze has covered Singapore. Thus, this project aims to accurately forecast regional air quality pollution levels across Singapore before the haze covers the island, by leveraging on temporal dependencies and cross-station spatial patterns. By providing the framework, it would help provide crucial preparation time to issue public health advisories, distribute masks, which ultimately mitigates acute respiratory and cardiovascular health risks. 

Our primary objective is to predict the West region's hourly PM$_2.5$ concentration at $t+1$ and $t+6$ hours from information observable by forecast origin $t$. West is a relevant case study given its location on Singapore's western side and our focus on haze associated with Sumatra. Readings from the other four regions are used as predictors. VARX and SAR model all five regions jointly, but their West-region forecasts are used for the main comparison. This choice does not assume that West is always the first or most polluted region.

The response is hourly PM$_{2.5}$ concentration, measured in $\mu\mathrm{g/m}^3$, rather than the Pollutant Standards Index (PSI). NEA reports one-hour PM$_{2.5}$ separately from the 24-hour PSI, which is an index based on several pollutants (National Environment Agency, n.d.). Our forecasts therefore concern short-term particulate concentrations, not the official PSI.

To assess short-term PM2.5 forecasting accuracy, out-of-sample Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for the West region of Singapore over the test window from 21 to 31 October 2019 (train set: 1 August to 20 October 2019) is the primary evaluation criterion. MAE directly measures the typical forecast error in concentration units without letting rare extreme spikes from dominating the ranking of the models. Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) and out-of-sample $R^2$ are reported in model-specific tables as supporting diagnostics of large-error sensitivity and variance explained relative to the test mean, while model selection across architectures is governed by Test MAE at the $t+1\text{ hr}$ and $t+6\text{ hr}$ horizons.

We evaluate both $t+1\text{ hr}$ and $t+6\text{ hr}$ horizons to compare short-horizon persistence against medium-horizon predictability. Although $t+1\text{ hr}$ offers limited lead time for timely advisories, it tests immediate tracking and spatial spillover, whereas $t+6\text{ hr}$ examines whether longer lead-time forecasts remain reliable as weather and smoke dynamics evolve.

# Data
The analyses uses 4 historical datasets compiled from official environmental monitoring networks and satellite remote sensing repositories. Regional air quality data which captures PM2.5 every hour, meteorological wind data which includes wind direction and wind speeds across Singapore are sourced from The National Environment Agency (NEA). Satellite fire hotspot data is obtained from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) fire archive. 

## Data Cleaning
Before analyzing, we cleaned the data to obtain a structured dataset. For satellite fire hotspot data, only those with a confidence score of 30% or higher were retained to eliminate false alarms. These fire records were then cleaned to only include the Sumatra region as the source based on their geographic coordinates. The records were aggregated daily to compute total Fire Radiative Power and cumulative fire counts. 

Meteorological wind data were cleaned by restricting the data to 5 representative monitoring stations in Singapore. Timestamps were standardized to uniform hourly blocks. To ensure wind dynamics could be interpreted linearly by the models, circular wind direction and wind speed were decomposed into orthogonal Cartesian velocity vectors. This gave East-West and North-South velocity components, where positive values represent winds from the South. 

Regional air quality data was filtered to only Southwest Monsoon haze window from 1 August to 31 October 2019. The hourly air quality data across all monitoring stations, hourly Cartesian wind vectors and daily Sumatra fire aggregates were merged based on the timestamps and dates. Since NASA FIRMS dataset only contains rows for days where a fire is detected, if a day has no fires, there will be no row for that date. Thus, when merging the datasets, any day without recorded fires will have a missing value. These missing values will be explicitly filled with 0, representing 0 fires on those dates.  

```{r data-import-and-cleaning, include=FALSE}
pm25_raw    <- read_csv("Historical1hrPM2.5.csv")
wind_dir   <- read_csv("HistoricalWindDirectionacrossSingapore2019.csv")
wind_spd   <- read_csv("HistoricalWindSpeedacrossSingapore2019.csv")
fire_raw   <- read_csv("fire_archive_M-C61_825464.csv")

# ==============================================================================
# 2. CLEAN & PROCESS NASA FIRMS FIRE HOTSPOTS
# ==============================================================================
fire_daily <- fire_raw %>%
  filter(confidence >= 30) %>%
  mutate(
    Date = ymd(acq_date),
    source_zone = case_when(
      latitude >= -6 & latitude <= 6  & longitude >= 95  & longitude <= 106 ~ "Sumatra",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(source_zone == "Sumatra") %>%
  group_by(Date, source_zone) %>%
  summarise(
    daily_frp   = sum(frp, na.rm = TRUE),
    daily_count = n(),
    .groups     = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = source_zone,
    values_from = c(daily_frp, daily_count),
    values_fill = 0
  )
# ==============================================================================
# 3. CLEAN & PROCESS WIND DATA (VECTOR DECOMPOSITION)
# ==============================================================================
target_stations <- c("S50", "S24", "S109", "S111", "S104") # Representative Singapore stations

# Standardize Wind Direction (Degrees)
clean_dir <- wind_dir %>%
  filter(station_id %in% target_stations) %>%
  mutate(
    Timestamp = floor_date(ymd_hms(timestamp), unit = "hour"),
    wind_dir_deg = as.numeric(reading_value)
  ) %>%
  group_by(Timestamp) %>%
  summarise(mean_wind_dir = mean(wind_dir_deg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Standardize Wind Speed (Knots)
clean_spd <- wind_spd %>%
  filter(station_id %in% target_stations) %>%
  mutate(
    Timestamp = floor_date(ymd_hms(timestamp), unit = "hour"),
    wind_spd_knot = as.numeric(reading_value)
  ) %>%
  group_by(Timestamp) %>%
  summarise(mean_wind_spd = mean(wind_spd_knot, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Merge wind tables and convert circular angles into Cartesian u and w vectors
wind_hourly <- inner_join(clean_dir, clean_spd, by = "Timestamp") %>%
  mutate(
    rad    = mean_wind_dir * pi / 180,
    # u component: East-West wind velocity vector
    wind_u = -mean_wind_spd * sin(rad),
    # w component: North-South wind velocity vector (positive = Southerly winds pushing towards SG)
    wind_w = -mean_wind_spd * cos(rad)
  )
```

# Feature Engineering
Raw polar coordinates of wind speed and direction were transformed into Cartesian vector components (wind_u and wind_w) using trigonometric conversion:
$$
\begin{aligned}
u &= -\text{speed} \cdot \sin(\theta) \\
w &= -\text{speed} \cdot \cos(\theta)
\end{aligned}
$$
This isolates the North-South velocity component where positive values represent Southern wind blowing northward. Alongside regional autoregressive lags (0–5 hours across the five regions) that capture short-term persistence and spatial spillover, an interaction term was also engineered to model the physical interaction between fire intensity and wind conditions. This means that Sumatra fire power only contributes to Singapore's pollution influx when southern winds blow northward:
$$\text{smoke\_transport\_Sumatra} = \max(0, \text{wind}_w) \times \text{daily\_frp\_Sumatra}$$

```{r features-and-master-table, include=FALSE}
# 4. CLEAN AIR QUALITY DATA & BUILD THE MASTER TABLE
# ==============================================================================
master_haze_2019 <- pm25_raw %>%
  rename(datetime_str = 1) %>%
  mutate(
    Timestamp = dmy_hm(datetime_str),
    Date = as_date(Timestamp)
  ) %>%
  # Filter strictly to the 2019 peak Southwest Monsoon haze window (Aug 1 - Oct 31)
  filter(year(Timestamp) == 2019, month(Timestamp) %in% 8:10) %>%
  dplyr::select(Timestamp, Date, north, south, east, west, central) %>%
  # Join hourly wind vectors
  left_join(wind_hourly, by = "Timestamp") %>%
  # Join daily Indonesian fire data
  left_join(fire_daily, by = "Date") %>%
  # Replace missing fire days with zero
  replace_na(list(
    daily_frp_Sumatra = 0, daily_frp_Kalimantan = 0,
    daily_count_Sumatra = 0, daily_count_Kalimantan = 0
  )) %>%
  # Create physics-based advection interaction term: Southerly wind * Sumatra Fire Power
  mutate(
    smoke_transport_Sumatra = pmax(0, wind_w) * daily_frp_Sumatra
  ) %>%
  arrange(Timestamp)

# Check final structure of your clean master data frame
dim(master_haze_2019)
head(master_haze_2019)



# ==============================================================================
```

# Methodologies 
## Elastic Net Regression (Baseline Regularized Model)
Elastic Net regularizes regression framework was implemented to forecast the West region's PM2.5 levels at $t+1$ hour and $t+6$ hours, while handling multicollinearity among spatial monitoring stations. Elastic Net combines both Lasso and Ridge penalties to perform simultaneous variable selection and coefficient shrinkage.

The feature space was constructed using temporal autoregressive lags across the 5 regional monitoring stations, spanning 0 to 5 hours and yielding 25 predictor variables. Prior to model fitting, all features were centered and scaled ($\text{preProcess} = c(\text{"scale"})$).

To prevent data leakage and simulate real-world forecasting performance during high-stakes pollution events, a strict chronological time-based split was enforced with 5-fold cross-validation over a grid of mixing parameters ($\alpha$) and penalty multipliers ($\lambda$).

```{r elastic-net-training, include=FALSE}
# PART 2: PHASE 2 - ELASTIC NET MODEL (t+1 and t+6 Horizons, MAE Metric)
# ==============================================================================

split_date <- ymd("2019-10-21")

# A. Original lagged observation function for regional PM2.5 readings
lagged_obs <- function(df, L) {
  if (L == 0) {
    return(df %>% dplyr::select(north, south, east, west, central))
  }
  df %>%
    transmute(across(c(north, south, east, west, central),
                     ~lag(., L),
                     .names = "Lag_{col}_{L}"))
}

# Function to run Elastic Net for any forecast horizon h (t+1 and t+6)
fit_elastic_net_horizon <- function(h, seed = 42) {

  cat(sprintf("\n========================================\n"))
  cat(sprintf("Running Elastic Net for Horizon: t+%d\n", h))
  cat(sprintf("========================================\n"))

  # Generate 0 to 5 hour regional lags and define target as lead(west, h)
  PM25_with_lags <- c(0, 1:5) %>%
    map_dfc(function(L) lagged_obs(master_haze_2019, L)) %>%
    mutate(
      Timestamp = master_haze_2019$Timestamp,
      target = lead(west, h)
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(Timestamp, target, starts_with("Lag")) %>%
    drop_na()

  # B. Chronological Time-Based Train-Test Split
  # Training window: August 1 to October 20
  # Testing window: October 21 to October 31
  train_data <- PM25_with_lags %>%
    filter(Timestamp < split_date) %>%
    dplyr::select(-Timestamp) # Remove timestamp column before modeling matrix

  test_data <- PM25_with_lags %>%
    filter(Timestamp >= split_date) %>%
    dplyr::select(-Timestamp)

  cat("Dimensions of training set:", dim(train_data), "\n")
  cat("Dimensions of testing set:", dim(test_data), "\n")

  # C. Train Elastic Net Model using caret (5-fold CV, scaling, hyperparameter grid)
  set.seed(seed) # Keep seed for cross-fold partitioning reproducibility only
  elastic_net_model <- train(
    target ~ .,
    data = train_data,
    method = "glmnet",
    tuneGrid = expand.grid(
      alpha = seq(from = 0, to = 1, length = 5),
      lambda = 10^(seq(from = -2, to = 2, length = 5))
    ),
    trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5),
    preProcess = c("scale")
  )

  # Print tuning summary and best hyperparameters found via cross-validation
  print(elastic_net_model)
  print(elastic_net_model$bestTune)

  # D. Evaluate on Out-of-Sample Test Set (MAE metric standardization)
  predictions <- predict(elastic_net_model, newdata = test_data)
  test_mae  <- MAE(predictions, test_data$target)

  cat(sprintf("--- Out-of-Sample Test Performance (t+%d) ---\n", h))
  cat("Test MAE:", test_mae, "\n")

   if (h == 1) {
    model_t1 <<- elastic_net_model
    test_mae_enet_t1 <<- test_mae
  } else if (h == 6) {
    model_t6 <<- elastic_net_model
    test_mae_enet_t6 <<- test_mae
  }
  # E. Extract Final Model Coefficients
  best_alpha <- elastic_net_model$bestTune$alpha
  best_lambda <- elastic_net_model$bestTune$lambda

  en_coefs <- coef(elastic_net_model$finalModel, s = best_lambda)
  print(en_coefs)

  # F. Visualisation: Coefficient Paths across Lambda (Lab 4 Style)
  lambda_for_plotting <- 10^seq(from = -2, to = 2, length = 100)

  en_path_model <- glmnet(
    x = as.matrix(scale(train_data %>% dplyr::select(-target))),
    y = train_data$target,
    alpha = best_alpha,
    lambda = lambda_for_plotting
  )

  en_path_df <- as.matrix(coef(en_path_model, lambda_for_plotting)) %>%
    t() %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    mutate(lambda = lambda_for_plotting)

  path_plot <- en_path_df %>%
    dplyr::select(-`(Intercept)`) %>%
    pivot_longer(-lambda, names_to = "variable", values_to = "coef") %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = lambda, y = coef, colour = variable)) +
    geom_line() +
    scale_x_log10() +
    labs(
      title = sprintf("Elastic Net Regularization Coefficient Paths (t+%d hr)", h),
      subtitle = sprintf("Optimal alpha = %.2f (Chronological Split)", best_alpha),
      x = "Lambda (log scale)",
      y = "Coefficient Estimate",
      colour = "Predictor"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

  print(path_plot)
  ggsave(
    sprintf("Elastic_Net_Coefficient_Paths_t%d.png", h),
    plot = path_plot, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300
  )

  tibble(horizon = paste0("t+", h, " hr"), model = "Elastic Net", MAE = test_mae)
}

# Run Elastic Net for both t+1 and t+6 horizons
horizons <- c(1, 6)
elastic_net_results <- map_dfr(horizons, fit_elastic_net_horizon)

print("\n--- Summary Table: Elastic Net Performance Across Horizons ---")
print(elastic_net_results)

# ==============================================================================
```

## Random Forest
A 500-tree Random Forest captures interactions and non-linear threshold that a simple linear regression might overlook (Breiman, 2001). The predictors include every lag, all wind variables and the **previous day** Sumatran fire/transport proxies. `mtry` is chosen from a predefined grid by out-of-bag (OOB) mean squared error (MSE) on the training data; the test set is used for final MAE. The OOB selection is not a chronological assessment and may favor temporally correlated features, therefore we treat the importance scores as model diagnostics rather than casual estimates.

```{r random-forest-training, include=FALSE}
# PHASE 3: Random Forest
# ==============================================================================
# install.packages("randomForest")
# Training set: August 1 to October 20, 2019
# Test set: October 21 to October 31, 2019
library(randomForest)

region_cols <- c("north", "south", "east", "west", "central")

exog_cols <- c(
  "wind_u", "wind_w", "mean_wind_spd",
  "daily_frp_Sumatra",
  "daily_count_Sumatra",
  "smoke_transport_Sumatra"
)

phase3_train_start <- as.POSIXct("2019-08-01 00:00:00", tz = "UTC")
phase3_test_start  <- as.POSIXct("2019-10-21 00:00:00", tz = "UTC")
phase3_test_end    <- as.POSIXct("2019-11-01 00:00:00", tz = "UTC")

build_horizon_data <- function(df, h, n_lags = 5) {
  lag_df <- map_dfc(0:n_lags, function(L) {
    df %>%
      transmute(
        across(
          all_of(region_cols),
          ~ dplyr::lag(.x, L),
          .names = paste0("Lag_{col}_", L)
        )
      )
  })

  bind_cols(
    tibble(
      Timestamp = df$Timestamp,
      target = dplyr::lead(df$west, h)
    ),
    lag_df,
    df %>% dplyr::select(all_of(exog_cols))
  ) %>%
    drop_na()
}

fit_horizon <- function(h, seed = 42) {
  d <- build_horizon_data(master_haze_2019, h)
  d$target_time <- d$Timestamp + lubridate::hours(h)

  train <- d %>%
    filter(
      target_time >= phase3_train_start,
      target_time < phase3_test_start
    )

  test <- d %>%
    filter(
      target_time >= phase3_test_start,
      target_time < phase3_test_end
    )

  if (nrow(train) == 0 || nrow(test) == 0) {
    stop(
      "Phase 3 produced an empty training or testing set for horizon t+",
      h,
      ". Check the Timestamp range and time zone."
    )
  }

  x_train <- train %>%
    dplyr::select(-Timestamp, -target, -target_time) %>%
    as.data.frame()

  x_test <- test %>%
    dplyr::select(-Timestamp, -target, -target_time) %>%
    as.data.frame()

  y_train <- train$target
  y_test  <- test$target

  cat("\nForecast horizon:", h, "hour(s)\n")
  cat(
    "Training target period:",
    format(min(train$target_time), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC"),
    "to",
    format(max(train$target_time), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC"),
    "\n"
  )
  cat(
    "Testing target period:",
    format(min(test$target_time), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC"),
    "to",
    format(max(test$target_time), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC"),
    "\n"
  )
  cat("Training observations:", nrow(train), "\n")
  cat("Testing observations:", nrow(test), "\n")

  p <- ncol(x_train)

  mtry_grid <- sort(unique(as.integer(
    pmax(1, pmin(p, round(c(sqrt(p), p / 5, p / 3, p / 2, p))))
  )))

  oob_tbl <- map_dfr(mtry_grid, function(m) {
    set.seed(seed)
    rf_m <- randomForest(
      x = x_train,
      y = y_train,
      ntree = 500,
      mtry = m
    )

    tibble(
      horizon = h,
      mtry = m,
      oob_mse = tail(rf_m$mse, 1)
    )
  })

  best_mtry <- oob_tbl$mtry[which.min(oob_tbl$oob_mse)]

  set.seed(seed)
  rf_final <- randomForest(
    x = x_train,
    y = y_train,
    ntree = 500,
    mtry = best_mtry,
    importance = TRUE
  )

  rf_pred <- predict(rf_final, newdata = x_test)

  set.seed(seed)
  en_fit <- train(
    x = x_train,
    y = y_train,
    method = "glmnet",
    tuneGrid = expand.grid(
      alpha = seq(0, 1, length = 5),
      lambda = 10^seq(-2, 2, length = 5)
    ),
    trControl = trainControl(
      method = "timeslice",
      initialWindow = floor(0.7 * nrow(x_train)),
      horizon = 24,
      fixedWindow = FALSE
    ),
    preProcess = c("scale")
  )

  en_pred <- predict(en_fit, newdata = x_test)

  naive_pred <- x_test$Lag_west_0

  metrics <- function(pred, obs, name) {
    tibble(
      horizon = h,
      model = name,
      RMSE = sqrt(mean((obs - pred)^2)),
      MAE = mean(abs(obs - pred)),
      R2 = 1 - sum((obs - pred)^2) /
        sum((obs - mean(obs))^2)
    )
  }

  results <- bind_rows(
    metrics(naive_pred, y_test, "Persistence (naive)"),
    metrics(en_pred,    y_test, "Elastic Net"),
    metrics(rf_pred,    y_test, "Random Forest")
  )

  imp <- importance(rf_final, type = 1) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column("variable") %>%
    rename(perm_importance = `%IncMSE`) %>%
    mutate(horizon = h)

  list(
    results = results,
    oob = oob_tbl,
    importance = imp,
    rf = rf_final,
    best_mtry = best_mtry,
    test_df = tibble(
      Timestamp = test$target_time,
      actual = y_test,
      rf = rf_pred,
      en = en_pred,
      horizon = h
    )
  )
}

horizons <- c(1, 6)
phase3_fit <- map(horizons, fit_horizon)
names(phase3_fit) <- paste0("t+", horizons)
```

## Support Vector Machine (SVM)
Support vector regression minimises model complexity subject to an $\varepsilon$-insensitive loss, allowing linear and kernel-based functional relationships. The data used for both SVM and Random Forest are the same. We test and compare linear, polynomial and radial kernels. All scaling is fitted within the training folds. The kernel and parameters with the lowest mean validation MAE are selected separately by horizon, refitted on all training data, and evaluated once on the untouched test set using MAE, RMSE and predictive $R^2$.

```{r svm-training, include=FALSE}
# SUPPORT VECTOR REGRESSION (SVM): adapted from mh4510_lab_06_svm.Rmd
# ==============================================================================
# The lab compares linear, polynomial and radial kernels with caret/kernlab.
# Here a numeric target invokes regression, with chronological resampling.
library(kernlab)
svm_region_cols <- c("north", "south", "east", "west", "central")
svm_exog_cols <- c("wind_u", "wind_w", "mean_wind_spd", "daily_frp_Sumatra",
                   "daily_count_Sumatra", "smoke_transport_Sumatra")

build_svm_data <- function(h) {
  lag_df <- map_dfc(0:5, function(L) {
    master_haze_2019 %>% transmute(across(all_of(svm_region_cols),
      ~ dplyr::lag(.x, L), .names = paste0("Lag_{col}_", L)))
  })
  bind_cols(tibble(Timestamp = master_haze_2019$Timestamp,
                   target_time = dplyr::lead(master_haze_2019$Timestamp, h),
                   target = dplyr::lead(master_haze_2019$west, h)),
            lag_df, master_haze_2019 %>% dplyr::select(all_of(svm_exog_cols))) %>%
    filter(target_time == Timestamp + hours(h)) %>% drop_na()
}

svm_grids <- list(
  Linear = list(method = "svmLinear", grid = expand.grid(C = 2^(-4:1))),
  Polynomial = list(method = "svmPoly",
    grid = expand.grid(C = c(0.5, 2), scale = c(1/64, 1/16), degree = c(2, 3))),
  Radial = list(method = "svmRadial",
    grid = expand.grid(sigma = c(1/16, 1/8, 1/4), C = c(0.5, 2)))
)

fit_svm_horizon <- function(h, seed = 42) {
  d <- build_svm_data(h)
  train <- d %>% filter(target_time >= phase3_train_start,
                        target_time < phase3_test_start)
  test <- d %>% filter(target_time >= phase3_test_start,
                       target_time < phase3_test_end)
  # Exactly the target observations used for the Phase 3 West forecasts.
  rf_test <- phase3_fit[[match(h, c(1, 6))]]$test_df
  stopifnot(identical(as.numeric(test$target_time), as.numeric(rf_test$Timestamp)),
            isTRUE(all.equal(test$target, rf_test$actual)))
  x_train <- train %>% dplyr::select(-Timestamp, -target_time, -target) %>% as.data.frame()
  x_test <- test %>% dplyr::select(-Timestamp, -target_time, -target) %>% as.data.frame()
  # Three expanding training windows followed by seven-day validation blocks.
  cutoffs <- as.POSIXct(c("2019-09-23", "2019-10-01", "2019-10-09"), tz = "UTC")
  index_out <- lapply(cutoffs, function(cut) which(train$target_time >= cut &
                                                  train$target_time < cut + days(7)))
  # Purge the boundary: every fitted target must precede the first validation origin.
  index <- lapply(index_out, function(ii) which(train$target_time < min(train$Timestamp[ii])))
  names(index) <- names(index_out) <- paste0("TimeBlock", seq_along(index))
  stopifnot(all(lengths(index) > 0), all(lengths(index_out) > 0))
  for (i in seq_along(index)) {
    stopifnot(max(train$target_time[index[[i]]]) < min(train$Timestamp[index_out[[i]]]))
  }
  control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 3, index = index, indexOut = index_out,
                          allowParallel = FALSE, returnResamp = "final", verboseIter = TRUE)
  candidates <- map(names(svm_grids), function(kernel) {
    spec <- svm_grids[[kernel]]
    cat("\nSVM horizon", h, "kernel", kernel, "\n")
    set.seed(seed)
    fit <- caret::train(x = x_train, y = train$target, method = spec$method,
      tuneGrid = spec$grid, trControl = control, metric = "MAE", maximize = FALSE,
      preProcess = c("zv", "center", "scale"))
    best <- fit$results
    for (parameter in names(fit$bestTune)) {
      best <- best[best[[parameter]] == fit$bestTune[[parameter]], , drop = FALSE]
    }
    list(kernel = kernel, fit = fit, cv_mae = best$MAE[1])
  })
  names(candidates) <- names(svm_grids)
  best_index <- which.min(map_dbl(candidates, "cv_mae"))
  winner <- candidates[[best_index]]
  # caret refits each tuned candidate on all training rows; only the CV winner
  # is evaluated on the untouched test set (no kernel selection on test errors).
  pred <- as.numeric(predict(winner$fit, newdata = x_test))
  stopifnot(length(pred) == nrow(test), all(is.finite(pred)))
  params <- winner$fit$bestTune
  param_text <- paste(paste(names(params), format(unlist(params), trim = TRUE), sep = "="),
                      collapse = ", ")
  tuning <- map_dfr(candidates, function(candidate) {
    as_tibble(candidate$fit$results) %>%
      mutate(horizon = paste0("t+", h, " hr"), kernel = candidate$kernel)
  })
  list(
    results = tibble(horizon = paste0("t+", h, " hr"), model = "SVM",
      RMSE = sqrt(mean((pred - test$target)^2)), MAE = mean(abs(pred - test$target)),
      R2 = 1 - sum((pred - test$target)^2) / sum((test$target - mean(test$target))^2)),
    selection = tibble(horizon = paste0("t+", h, " hr"), kernel = winner$kernel,
      Parameters = param_text, Validation_MAE = winner$cv_mae,
      Training_n = nrow(train), Testing_n = nrow(test)),
    tuning = tuning, model = winner$fit,
    kernel_summary = tibble(horizon = paste0("t+", h, " hr"),
      kernel = names(candidates), Validation_MAE = map_dbl(candidates, "cv_mae")),
    forecasts = tibble(Timestamp = test$target_time, Actual = test$target,
      SVM = pred, Persistence = test$Lag_west_0, horizon = paste0("t+", h, " hr")),
    resampling = list(index = index, indexOut = index_out)
  )
}

svm_fit <- map(c(1, 6), fit_svm_horizon)
svm_results <- map_dfr(svm_fit, "results")
svm_selection <- map_dfr(svm_fit, "selection")
svm_tuning <- map_dfr(svm_fit, "tuning")
svm_kernel_summary <- map_dfr(svm_fit, "kernel_summary")
svm_forecasts <- map_dfr(svm_fit, "forecasts")
print(svm_results)
print(svm_selection)
print(svm_kernel_summary)

svm_forecast_plot <- svm_forecasts %>%
  pivot_longer(c(Actual, SVM, Persistence), names_to = "Series", values_to = "PM25") %>%
  ggplot(aes(Timestamp, PM25, colour = Series, linetype = Series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.45) + facet_wrap(~ horizon, ncol = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Actual = "black", SVM = "#0072B2", Persistence = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Actual = "solid", SVM = "solid", Persistence = "dotted")) +
  labs(title = "SVM Forecasts vs Actual PM2.5: West", x = "Target timestamp",
       y = "PM2.5 (ug/m3)", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
print(svm_forecast_plot)
ggsave("SVM_Forecast_vs_Actual.png", svm_forecast_plot, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)

svm_kernel_plot <- ggplot(svm_kernel_summary, aes(kernel, Validation_MAE, colour = horizon)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)) +
  labs(title = "SVM Kernel Selection", subtitle = "Best mean validation MAE per kernel across three chronological blocks",
       x = "Kernel", y = "Validation MAE (ug/m3)", colour = "Horizon") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
ggsave("SVM_Kernel_Validation.png", svm_kernel_plot, width = 8, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
write_csv(svm_results, "SVM_Test_Metrics.csv")
write_csv(svm_selection, "SVM_Selected_Models.csv")
write_csv(svm_tuning, "SVM_Tuning_Results.csv")
write_csv(svm_forecasts, "SVM_Test_Forecasts.csv")
saveRDS(list(results = svm_results, selection = svm_selection, tuning = svm_tuning,
             kernel_summary = svm_kernel_summary, forecasts = svm_forecasts, fits = svm_fit),
        "SVM_Analysis_Outputs.rds")

# ==============================================================================
```

## VARX Spatio-Temporal Model
### Model Formulation & Estimation
To model Singapore's five regional air quality series simultaneously rather than in isolation, we implement a Vector Autoregressive Exogenous ($\text{VARX}(p)$) system to capture inter-regional temporal dependencies across the island alongside external wind and fire conditions:

$$Y_t = c + \sum_{i=1}^{p} A_i Y_{t-i} + B X_t + \varepsilon_t$$

where:

* $Y_t = [\text{North}_t, \text{South}_t, \text{East}_t, \text{West}_t, \text{Central}_t]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^5$ is the endogenous vector of hourly regional $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ concentrations.
* $X_t = [\text{wind\_u}_t, \text{wind\_w}_t, \text{daily\_frp\_Sumatra}_t, \text{smoke\_transport\_Sumatra}_t]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^4$ is the exogenous vector capturing East-West and North-South wind velocity components, daily Sumatran Fire Radiative Power (FRP), and wind-driven smoke advection.
* $c$ is a $5 \times 1$ intercept vector, $A_i$ are $5 \times 5$ endogenous lag coefficient matrices capturing inter-regional diffusion, $B$ is a $5 \times 4$ exogenous impact matrix, and $\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma_\varepsilon)$ is a $5 \times 1$ vector white-noise innovation process with covariance matrix $\Sigma_\varepsilon$.

Unlike univariate regressions that ignore cross-regional feedback, each matrix $A_i$ explicitly parameterises how lagged pollution in region $j$ affects region $k$ at time $t$. Since all five regional equations share the same set of lagged endogenous and exogenous regressors, estimating each region's equation via Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) is equivalent to Generalised Least Squares (GLS) and yields consistent, asymptotically efficient estimates of $\hat{c}$, $\hat{A}_1, \dots, \hat{A}_p$, and $\hat{B}$.

### Stationarity Verification & Lag Order Selection
Valid VAR estimation requires all endogenous series in $Y_t$ to be covariance-stationary so that parameter estimates remain time-invariant and impulse responses decay rather than diverge. Prior to fitting the model on the training set ($n = 1,944$ hourly observations), we apply the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test to each regional series in $Y_{\text{train}}$. We then select the optimal lag order $p \in \{1, \dots, 10\}$ by minimising the Akaike Information Criterion, balancing multivariate goodness-of-fit against parameter complexity.

### Spatial Transmission & Diffusion Indicators
To test our physical advection hypothesis under the Southwest Monsoon, we conduct two structural diagnostics on the fitted $\text{VARX}(p)$ system:

1. Granger Causality Tests: Using a joint Wald $F$-test, we test the null hypothesis that all lag coefficients from an upwind source region $j$ to the remaining regions $k \neq j$ are jointly zero ($A_{1,kj} = \dots = A_{p,kj} = 0$). Rejecting this null confirms that upwind $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ readings improve predictions of downwind pollution beyond the downwind zones' own autoregressive history.
2. Orthogonalised Impulse Response Functions (IRFs): As contemporaneous innovations $\varepsilon_t$ are correlated across Singapore's closely spaced monitoring zones, simulating a shock to one element of $\varepsilon_t$ in isolation would be physically unrealistic. Hence, we apply a Cholesky decomposition ($\Sigma_\varepsilon = P P^\top$) to orthogonalise the innovations into independent structural shocks $u_t = P^{-1}\varepsilon_t$. Rewriting the system in its moving-average representation traces how a smoke shock entering South or West propagates across all five regions over a 24-hour window (with 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals).

### Out-of-Sample Forecast Evaluation
To ensure a direct, leak-free comparison with the other models in this study, we evaluate the fitted $\text{VARX}(p)$ system chronologically on the untouched holdout test window. At each forecast origin $t$, we recursively generate multi-step predictions for both short-term ($t+1\text{ hr}$) and medium-term ($t+6\text{ hr}$) horizons using the estimated coefficient matrices $\hat{A}_1, \dots, \hat{A}_p$ and $\hat{B}$.

```{r varx-training, include=FALSE}
# PHASE 4 -  VECTOR AUTOREGRESSIVE EXOGENOUS (VARX) SYSTEM ----
# ==============================================================================
# install.packages("vars")
# install.packages("tseries")
library(vars)
library(tseries)

# 1. Train/Test sets (Chronological Split) ----

# Training set: August 1 to October 20, 2019
# Test set: October 21 to October 31, 2019
train_df <- master_haze_2019 %>% filter(Timestamp < as.POSIXct("2019-10-21 00:00:00", tz = "UTC"))
test_df  <- master_haze_2019 %>% filter(Timestamp >= as.POSIXct("2019-10-21 00:00:00", tz = "UTC"))
cat("VARX Training observations:", nrow(train_df), "\n")
cat("VARX Testing observations: ", nrow(test_df), "\n")
region_cols <- c("north", "south", "east", "west", "central")
exog_cols   <- c("wind_u", "wind_w", "daily_frp_Sumatra", "smoke_transport_Sumatra")

# Extract Endogenous Matrix Y_t and Exogenous Matrix X_t
Y_train <- as.matrix(train_df[, region_cols])
X_train <- as.matrix(train_df[, exog_cols])
Y_full  <- as.matrix(master_haze_2019[, region_cols])
X_full  <- as.matrix(master_haze_2019[, exog_cols])

# 2. Stationarity Checks (Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test) ----

apply(Y_train, 2, function(x) {
  adf_res <- adf.test(x)
  return(c(p_value = adf_res$p.value))
  })

# 3. Optimal Lag Selection & VARX Fit ----

# Determine optimal lag length (p) using AIC/BIC
lag_selection <- VARselect(Y_train, lag.max = 10, type = "const", exogen = X_train)
print(lag_selection$selection)
optimal_p <- lag_selection$selection["AIC(n)"]
cat("Selected Optimal Lag p (AIC):", optimal_p, "\n")

# Fit the VARX(p) System
varx_fit <- VAR(Y_train, p = optimal_p, type = "const", exogen = X_train)
summary(varx_fit) # Fits linear regression equations for each region

# 4. Granger Causality Tests ----
# (To test directional transmission across regions under prevailing winds,
#   specifically South and West due to the Southwest Monsoon)

for (reg in region_cols) {
  cat("\nGranger Causality - Cause:", reg, "\n")
  print(causality(varx_fit, cause = reg)$Granger)
}

# 5. Impulse Response Functions (IRF Simulation) ----
# (Traces how an incoming smoke shock at the South/West diffuses across Singapore)

# South
irf_south <- irf(
  varx_fit,
  impulse = "south",
  response = c("north", "south", "east", "west", "central"),
  n.ahead = 24, # 24-hour diffusion window
  boot = TRUE,
  ci = 0.95
)
plot(irf_south, main = "Island-Wide PM2.5 Response to South Shock (24-Hour Horizon)")

png("VARX_South_IRF.png", width = 8, height = 10, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(irf_south, main = "Island-Wide PM2.5 Response to South Shock (24-Hour Horizon)")
dev.off()

# West
irf_west <- irf(
  varx_fit,
  impulse = "west",
  response = c("north", "south", "east", "west", "central"),
  n.ahead = 24, # 24-hour diffusion window
  boot = TRUE,
  ci = 0.95
)
plot(irf_west, main = "Island-Wide PM2.5 Response to West Shock (24-Hour Horizon)")

png("VARX_West_IRF.png", width = 8, height = 10, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(irf_west, main = "Island-Wide PM2.5 Response to West Shock (24-Hour Horizon)")
dev.off()

# 6. Forecasting & Evaluation on test set (t+1 and t+6) ----

# Extract coefficient matrices from fitted VARX(p) model:
# Y_t = c + A_1 Y_{t-1} + ... + A_p Y_{t-p} + B X_t
A_mats <- Acoef(varx_fit) # List of p (5x5) endogenous lag coefficient matrices
B_mat  <- Bcoef(varx_fit) # (5 x (5p + 1 + k_exog)) full coefficient matrix

# Separate intercept and exogenous coefficient matrices
const_vec <- B_mat[, "const"]
exog_mat  <- B_mat[, exog_cols, drop = FALSE]

# Helper function to recursively forecast h steps ahead from every origin t in test window
forecast_varx_horizon <- function(h) {
  # Indices in master_haze_2019 corresponding to target_time in Oct 21 - Oct 31
  target_indices <- which(
    master_haze_2019$Timestamp >= as.POSIXct("2019-10-21 00:00:00", tz = "UTC") &
      master_haze_2019$Timestamp <  as.POSIXct("2019-11-01 00:00:00", tz = "UTC")
  )

  preds_west  <- numeric(length(target_indices))
  actual_west <- numeric(length(target_indices))
  target_ts   <- master_haze_2019$Timestamp[target_indices]

  for (i in seq_along(target_indices)) {
    idx_target <- target_indices[i]
    idx_origin <- idx_target - h # Information available up to time t
    # History buffer of last p observed Y vectors: Y_{t}, Y_{t-1}, ..., Y_{t-p+1}
    Y_hist <- Y_full[(idx_origin - optimal_p + 1):idx_origin, , drop = FALSE]
    # Recursively step forward from step 1 to step h
    for (step in 1:h) {
      idx_step <- idx_origin + step
      x_step   <- X_full[idx_step, ]
      # Start with intercept + exogenous effect
      y_next <- const_vec + as.vector(exog_mat %*% x_step)
      # Add autoregressive lag contributions: sum_{L=1}^p A_L * Y_{idx_step - L}
      for (L in 1:optimal_p) {
        y_lag  <- Y_hist[nrow(Y_hist) - L + 1, ]
        y_next <- y_next + as.vector(A_mats[[L]] %*% y_lag)
      }
      # Append predicted y_next to history buffer for multi-step recursion
      Y_hist <- rbind(Y_hist, y_next)
    }
    preds_west[i]  <- tail(Y_hist, 1)[, "west"]
    actual_west[i] <- Y_full[idx_target, "west"]
  }

  rmse <- sqrt(mean((preds_west - actual_west)^2))
  mae  <- mean(abs(preds_west - actual_west))
  r2   <- 1 - sum((actual_west - preds_west)^2) / sum((actual_west - mean(actual_west))^2)

  list(
    metrics = tibble(
      horizon = paste0("t+", h, " hr"),
      model   = "VARX",
      RMSE    = rmse,
      MAE     = mae,
      R2      = r2
    ),
    df = tibble(
      Timestamp = target_ts,
      Actual    = actual_west,
      VARX_Predicted = preds_west,
      horizon   = paste0("t+", h, " hr")
    )
  )
}

# Run t+1 and t+6 forecasts
varx_h1 <- forecast_varx_horizon(1)
varx_h6 <- forecast_varx_horizon(6)
phase4_results <- bind_rows(varx_h1$metrics, varx_h6$metrics)
print(phase4_results) # MAE is 4.45 and 6.86 for t+1 and t+6 respectively
```

## Spatial Autoregressive
SAR predicts the five regional PM$_{2.5}$ values together, allowing linked regions to have related future outcomes:

$$\mathbf y_{t+h}=\rho_hW\mathbf y_{t+h}+X_t\boldsymbol\beta_h+\boldsymbol\varepsilon_{t+h},\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf y}_{t+h}=(I-\widehat\rho_hW)^{-1}X_t\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_h.$$

Here, $X_t$ contains current local pollution, wind components, Sumatra fire power and regional indicators. The fixed matrix $W$ averages linked neighbours: Central connects to all outer regions, and each outer region connects to Central and two other outer regions. The same weights are used at both horizons, without hyperparameter tuning. Shared slopes describe the input relationships, while regional indicators allow different starting levels.

Future neighbouring outcomes contain some of the same unexplained variation as the outcome being predicted. This breaks the OLS requirement that predictors are uncorrelated with the errors. SAR instead solves the five equations together. The inverse in the forecast equation includes both neighbour effects and feedback through further connections. Consequently, a regression coefficient alone does not give the full prediction change (Bivand and Piras, 2015).

Our maximum-likelihood implementation tries a value of $\rho$, fits the regression to $\mathbf y-\rho W\mathbf y$, and searches for the best likelihood. After estimating the regression coefficients and error variance for each candidate, it minimises

$$Q(\rho)=\frac{N}{2}\log\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{RSS}(\rho)}{N}\right)-T\log|\det(I-\rho W)|,$$

where $T$ is the number of training timestamps, $N=5T$, and RSS is the remaining squared error. The first term measures unexplained variation; the second accounts for the connected outcomes. This assumes independent Gaussian errors with a common variance. Restricting $|\rho|<1$ gives a unique solution for our row-standardised weights. Parameters are assumed stable over the study window.

Separate one- and six-hour models use training targets before 21 October 2019 and test targets on 21--31 October. Forecasts use current inputs, without observed future neighbours. West-region MAE is compared with OLS using the same inputs and test observations.

```{r sar-training, include=FALSE}
# PHASE 5: SPATIAL AUTOREGRESSIVE MODEL (SAR)
# ==============================================================================
# Fit the original fixed-neighbour SAR model by pooled Gaussian maximum
# likelihood in base R. No spatial-weight or other hyperparameter tuning.
regions <- c("north", "south", "east", "west", "central")
W <- matrix(0, 5, 5, dimnames = list(regions, regions))
W["north", c("east", "west", "central")] <- 1
W["south", c("east", "west", "central")] <- 1
W["east", c("north", "south", "central")] <- 1
W["west", c("north", "south", "central")] <- 1
W["central", c("north", "south", "east", "west")] <- 1
W <- W / rowSums(W)
sar_test_start <- as.POSIXct("2019-10-21", tz = "UTC")
formula_sp <- target ~ pm25 + wind_u + wind_w + fire_frp + region

build_sar_data <- function(h) {
  d <- master_haze_2019 %>%
    arrange(Timestamp) %>%
    mutate(future_time = lead(Timestamp, h),
           across(all_of(regions), ~ lead(.x, h), .names = "future_{.col}")) %>%
    filter(future_time == Timestamp + hours(h)) %>%
    drop_na(all_of(c(regions, paste0("future_", regions), "wind_u", "wind_w",
                     "daily_frp_Sumatra")))
  map_dfr(regions, function(r) {
    tibble(Timestamp = d$Timestamp, target_time = d$future_time,
           region = r, target = d[[paste0("future_", r)]], pm25 = d[[r]],
           wind_u = d$wind_u, wind_w = d$wind_w,
           fire_frp = d$daily_frp_Sumatra)
  }) %>%
    mutate(region = factor(region, levels = regions)) %>%
    arrange(region, Timestamp)
}

fit_pooled_sar <- function(d, weights) {
  X <- model.matrix(formula_sp, data = d)
  y <- d$target
  groups <- split(seq_len(nrow(d)), d$Timestamp)
  stopifnot(all(vapply(groups, length, integer(1)) == length(regions)))
  Wy <- numeric(length(y))
  for (ii in groups) {
    ii <- ii[order(d$region[ii])]
    stopifnot(identical(as.character(d$region[ii]), regions))
    Wy[ii] <- as.vector(weights %*% y[ii])
  }
  qrX <- qr(X)
  if (qrX$rank != ncol(X)) stop("SAR design matrix is rank deficient.")
  ey <- qr.resid(qrX, y)
  ew <- qr.resid(qrX, Wy)
  n <- length(y)
  nt <- length(groups)
  # Profile negative log-likelihood, omitting constants. For fixed rho,
  # beta is OLS of (y-rho*Wy) on X and sigma^2 is the residual MSE.
  nll <- function(rho) {
    rss <- sum((ey - rho * ew)^2)
    ld <- determinant(diag(5) - rho * weights, logarithm = TRUE)
    if (ld$sign <= 0 || rss <= 0) return(Inf)
    n / 2 * log(rss / n) - nt * as.numeric(ld$modulus)
  }
  opt <- optimize(nll, interval = c(-0.995, 0.995), tol = 1e-9)
  rho <- opt$minimum
  beta <- qr.coef(qrX, y - rho * Wy)
  # Numerical check: the optimum must be no worse than a coarse search.
  stopifnot(opt$objective <= min(vapply(seq(-0.99, 0.99, length.out = 101),
                                       nll, numeric(1))) + 1e-6)
  list(arcoef = rho, coefficients = beta, weights = weights,
       sigma2 = sum((ey - rho * ew)^2) / n,
       method = "Pooled Gaussian SAR maximum likelihood with fixed neighbours")
}

predict_pooled_sar <- function(model, d) {
  d %>% group_split(Timestamp) %>% map_dfr(function(g) {
    g <- arrange(g, region)
    stopifnot(identical(as.character(g$region), regions))
    X <- model.matrix(delete.response(terms(formula_sp)), data = g)
    xb <- as.vector(X[, names(model$coefficients), drop = FALSE] %*%
                      model$coefficients)
    g$prediction <- as.vector(solve(diag(5) - model$arcoef * model$weights, xb))
    # Confirm that the joint predictions satisfy the fitted equations.
    stopifnot(max(abs(g$prediction - model$arcoef *
                       as.vector(model$weights %*% g$prediction) - xb)) < 1e-7)
    g
  }) %>% arrange(region, Timestamp)
}

sar_metrics <- function(predictions, h) {
  map_dfr(c("OLS", "SAR"), function(m) {
    pred <- predictions[[m]]
    obs <- predictions$target
    tibble(Horizon = paste0("t+", h, " hr"), Model = m,
           RMSE = sqrt(mean((pred - obs)^2)), MAE = mean(abs(pred - obs)),
           R2 = cor(pred, obs)^2,
           Predictive_R2 = 1 - sum((pred - obs)^2) / sum((obs - mean(obs))^2))
  })
}

fit_sar <- function(h) {
  d <- build_sar_data(h)
  train_sp <- filter(d, target_time < sar_test_start)
  test_sp <- filter(d, target_time >= sar_test_start)
  stopifnot(nrow(train_sp) > 0, nrow(test_sp) > 0)
  # The same original neighbour matrix is used at both horizons.
  # Rho and regression coefficients are estimated, not hyperparameters tuned.
  sar <- fit_pooled_sar(train_sp, W)
  ols <- lm(formula_sp, data = train_sp)
  forecasts <- predict_pooled_sar(sar, test_sp) %>%
    rename(SAR = prediction) %>%
    mutate(OLS = as.numeric(predict(ols, newdata = .)),
           Horizon = paste0("t+", h, " hr"))
  list(results = sar_metrics(filter(forecasts, region == "west"), h),
       pooled_results = sar_metrics(forecasts, h),
       rho = sar$arcoef, sar_model = sar, ols_model = ols,
       forecasts = forecasts)
}

phase5_fit <- map(c(1, 6), fit_sar)
names(phase5_fit) <- c("t+1 hr", "t+6 hr")
# Primary scores use West, matching Phases 3 and 4. Keep pooled scores separate.
phase5_results <- map_dfr(phase5_fit, "results")
phase5_pooled_results <- map_dfr(phase5_fit, "pooled_results")
phase5_forecasts <- map_dfr(phase5_fit, "forecasts")
phase5_spatial <- map_dfr(seq_along(phase5_fit), function(i) {
  fit <- phase5_fit[[i]]
  tibble(Horizon = names(phase5_fit)[i], rho = fit$rho)
})
print(phase5_results)
print(phase5_pooled_results)
print(phase5_spatial)

sar_forecast_plot <- phase5_forecasts %>% filter(region == "west") %>%
  dplyr::select(target_time, Horizon, Actual = target, OLS, SAR) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(Actual, OLS, SAR), names_to = "Series", values_to = "PM25") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = target_time, y = PM25, colour = Series, linetype = Series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.45) + facet_wrap(~ Horizon, ncol = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Actual = "black", OLS = "#D55E00", SAR = "#0072B2")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Actual = "solid", OLS = "dotted", SAR = "solid")) +
  labs(title = "SAR and OLS Forecasts vs Actual PM2.5: West",
       subtitle = "Held-out target period: 21-31 October 2019",
       x = "Target timestamp", y = "PM2.5 (ug/m3)", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
print(sar_forecast_plot)
ggsave("SAR_Forecast_vs_Actual.png", sar_forecast_plot, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)

sar_regional_plot <- phase5_forecasts %>%
  dplyr::select(target_time, region, Horizon, Actual = target, SAR) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(Actual, SAR), names_to = "Series", values_to = "PM25") %>%
  ggplot(aes(target_time, PM25, colour = Series)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.35) +
  facet_grid(region ~ Horizon) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Actual = "black", SAR = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(title = "SAR Forecasts Across All Five Regions", x = "Target timestamp",
       y = "PM2.5 (ug/m3)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
ggsave("SAR_Regional_Forecasts.png", sar_regional_plot, width = 12, height = 10, dpi = 300)

sar_spatial_plot <- ggplot(phase5_spatial, aes(x = Horizon, y = rho)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2", width = 0.45) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("rho = %.3f", rho)), vjust = -0.5, size = 4) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)) +
  labs(title = "Spatial Dependence at Each Forecast Horizon",
       subtitle = "The same fixed neighbour links are used for both models",
       x = "Forecast horizon", y = "Estimated spatial coefficient (rho)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
print(sar_spatial_plot)
ggsave("SAR_Spatial_Coefficient.png", sar_spatial_plot, width = 8, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
```

```{r sar-implementation-checks, include=FALSE}
# SAR THEORY CHECKS: prediction sensitivity and recovery of known parameters.
# These explain the fitted model; they do not change training or tune W.
sar_sensitivity <- map_dfr(seq_along(phase5_fit), function(i) {
  fit <- phase5_fit[[i]]
  origin <- min(fit$forecasts$Timestamp)
  baseline <- fit$forecasts %>% filter(Timestamp == origin) %>% arrange(region)
  changed <- baseline %>% mutate(pm25 = pm25 + if_else(region == "west", 10, 0))
  before <- predict_pooled_sar(fit$sar_model, baseline)
  after <- predict_pooled_sar(fit$sar_model, changed)
  delta <- after$prediction - before$prediction
  # An independent calculation checks the spatial-multiplier interpretation.
  input_change <- 10 * fit$sar_model$coefficients["pm25"] * as.numeric(regions == "west")
  stopifnot(max(abs(delta - as.vector(solve(diag(5) - fit$rho * W, input_change)))) < 1e-8)
  tibble(Horizon = names(phase5_fit)[i], region = factor(regions, levels = regions),
         change = delta, type = if_else(regions == "west", "West (direct)", "Other regions"),
         regression_only = as.numeric(input_change))
})
sar_sensitivity_summary <- sar_sensitivity %>% group_by(Horizon) %>%
  summarise(West_change = change[region == "west"],
            West_without_feedback = regression_only[region == "west"],
            Largest_other_change = max(change[region != "west"]), .groups = "drop")
sar_sensitivity_plot <- ggplot(sar_sensitivity, aes(region, change, fill = type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) + geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", change)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ Horizon) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("West (direct)" = "#0072B2", "Other regions" = "#999999")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = tools::toTitleCase) +
  labs(title = "Forecast Change After Increasing Current West PM2.5 by 10",
       x = NULL, y = "Change in predicted PM2.5 (ug/m3)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
ggsave("SAR_Prediction_Changes.png", sar_sensitivity_plot, width = 8, height = 3.2,
       dpi = 300)

# Conditional simulation: independent Gaussian errors and known fixed W.
# This checks estimation, not forecasting performance on real haze data.
set.seed(2026)
sar_simulation_runs <- 100L
sar_simulation_times <- 200L
sar_simulation <- map_dfr(seq_len(sar_simulation_runs), function(replication) {
  times <- as.POSIXct("2019-08-01", tz = "UTC") + 3600 * seq_len(sar_simulation_times)
  inputs <- tibble(Timestamp = times, wind_u = rnorm(length(times)),
                   wind_w = rnorm(length(times)), fire_frp = rexp(length(times)))
  d <- map_dfr(regions, function(r) mutate(inputs, region = r)) %>%
    mutate(region = factor(region, levels = regions), pm25 = runif(n(), 5, 30),
           target = 0, target_time = Timestamp + hours(1))
  X <- model.matrix(formula_sp, data = d)
  beta <- setNames(c(2, 0.7, 0.2, -0.3, 0.1, 0.5, -0.4, 0.3, 0.1), colnames(X))
  rhs <- matrix(as.vector(X %*% beta) + rnorm(nrow(d)), nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE)
  d$target <- as.vector(t(solve(diag(5) - 0.4 * W, rhs)))
  estimated <- fit_pooled_sar(d, W)
  tibble(Replication = replication, rho = estimated$arcoef,
         pm25_coefficient = unname(estimated$coefficients["pm25"]))
})
sar_simulation_summary <- bind_rows(
  transmute(sar_simulation, Parameter = "rho", Estimate = rho),
  transmute(sar_simulation, Parameter = "pm25_coefficient", Estimate = pm25_coefficient)
) %>%
  mutate(True = if_else(Parameter == "rho", 0.4, 0.7)) %>%
  group_by(Parameter, True) %>%
  summarise(Mean_estimate = mean(Estimate),
            Estimation_RMSE = sqrt(mean((Estimate - True)^2)), .groups = "drop")
stopifnot(all(is.finite(sar_simulation$rho)),
          max(abs(sar_simulation_summary$Mean_estimate - sar_simulation_summary$True)) < 0.05)
print(sar_sensitivity_summary)
print(sar_simulation_summary)
write_csv(sar_sensitivity, "SAR_Prediction_Changes.csv")
write_csv(sar_simulation, "SAR_Simulation_Runs.csv")
write_csv(sar_simulation_summary, "SAR_Simulation_Summary.csv")
saveRDS(list(sensitivity = sar_sensitivity, sensitivity_summary = sar_sensitivity_summary,
             simulation = sar_simulation, simulation_summary = sar_simulation_summary),
        "SAR_Theory_Checks.rds")

write_csv(phase5_results, "SAR_Test_Metrics_West.csv")
write_csv(phase5_pooled_results, "SAR_Test_Metrics_All_Regions.csv")
write_csv(phase5_spatial, "SAR_Spatial_Coefficients.csv")
write_csv(phase5_forecasts, "SAR_Test_Forecasts.csv")
saveRDS(list(results = phase5_results, pooled_results = phase5_pooled_results,
             spatial = phase5_spatial,
             forecasts = phase5_forecasts, fits = phase5_fit), "SAR_Analysis_Outputs.rds")
# Keep compact objects needed to render the report without rerunning training.
saveRDS(mget(c("long_data","regional_summary", "driver_summary", "model_t1", "model_t6", "elastic_net_results",
               "phase3_results", "phase3_group", "phase3_oob", "phase3_fit",
               "svm_results", "svm_selection", "svm_kernel_summary", "svm_forecasts",
               "phase4_results", "phase5_results", "phase5_pooled_results",
               "phase5_spatial", "phase5_forecasts", "sar_sensitivity",
               "sar_sensitivity_summary", "sar_simulation_summary")),
```

# Results
## Elastic Net
Through 5-fold cross-validation, the model selected optimal tuning parameters of $\alpha = 0.5$ and $\lambda = 0.1$. This configuration reflects an even mixture of $L_1$ (Lasso) feature selection and $L_2$ (Ridge) coefficient shrinkage. The model achieved an out-of-sample Test MAE of 5.44 while the sparse coefficient matrix reveals that short-term pollutant persistence is heavily affected by immediate temporal proximity. Specifically, 1-hour historical lags have the strongest positive coefficients. Higher-order temporal lags (such as lags 3 to 5) were heavily shrunk or driven entirely to zero, indicating that immediate 1-hour momentum dictates short-horizon air quality states.
```{r enet-coef-t1, include = FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(Matrix)

best_lambda <- model_t1$bestTune$lambda
coef_mat_t1 <- as.matrix(coef(model_t1$finalModel, s = best_lambda))

coef_df_t1 <- data.frame(
  Feature = rownames(coef_mat_t1),
  Coefficient = round(coef_mat_t1[, 1], 4)
)
```


```{r enet-table-t1, include=FALSE}
# This chunk has NO include=FALSE. It only outputs the kable table cleanly.
knitr::kable(
  coef_df_t1,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  col.names = c("Predictor Feature", "Coefficient"),
  caption = "Elastic Net Sparse Coefficient Estimates (t+1 Horizon)",
  align = c("l", "c")
)
cat("\n\\normalsize\n")

```


```{r enet-path-t1, include=FALSE}
# Directly plot the glmnet regularization path from the final model
plot(model_t1$finalModel, xvar = "lambda", label = FALSE)
```

At the multi-step 6-hour horizon, cross-validation selected $\alpha = 0$ and $\lambda = 1$. This parameter combination collapses the Elastic Net penalty into pure Ridge regression. The model achieved an out-of-sample Test MAE of 7.38. As expected, predicting further into the future leads to larger errors because unpredictable weather shifts accumulate over time. Unlike the sparse feature selection observed at $t+1$, the multi-step horizon benefited from retaining all 25 lagged predictors without aggressive feature zeroing. Since predicting PM2.5 levels at $t+6$ hours requires capturing complex, island-wide weather patterns, retaining all past time data rather helps the model stay stable against sudden wind or weather changes.
